speaker: Sam Schrager
words: This conversation with Marie Leitch Fisher took place at her home in Lewiston on October 29, 1975. How do you wind up there in the mid-20s when you came?

speaker: Marie Leitch Fisher
words: Well, I had a cousin who lived there and I guess I just applied for the job and got it and went up. Those days you'd write applications telling what your qualifications were, what you could teach, and that's all I did and I got the job.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Where were you living at the time?

speaker: Marie Leitch Fisher
words: Well, my folks were living at Nez Perce, but I was only there during the summers, so I didn't really live much of anywhere. Wherever my trunk was, that's where I lived.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you taught before you came to Lewiston?

speaker: Marie Leitch Fisher
words: Oh yes, I taught. Oh, I must have taught 10 or 15 years, I guess, before I went to Lewiston. No, I hadn't taught that long. I taught about eight years before I went there, so I had experience and pretty good recommendations, I guess, because I got the job without any trouble. I taught primary for four years, and then they transferred me to the fifth and sixth, and then I taught the seventh and eighth, so I taught all of them.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Is this all in Bovill  or before you came?

speaker: Marie Leitch Fisher
words: No, in Bovill, but I taught rural schools and two-room schools before I went to Bovill.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Oh yes, I was going to ask you too, now you got your teacher training in Lewiston?

speaker: Marie Leitch Fisher
words: In the normal over here, yes.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How long did that take in those days?

speaker: Marie Leitch Fisher
words: Well, when I started out, all you had to do was go to summer school, which lasted, I think, nine weeks, something like that, and you got what was called a third grade certificate. Then you'd teach that on that third grade certificate that year, and then you'd go back to summer school, and then you got a second grade, and then you'd go back to summer school next year, and you'd get a first grade, and then you had your certificate. But the people that wanted to go to school, if they'd take a whole year at once, why they didn't have to go through that? I couldn't be bothered going a whole year, and I could go nine weeks and get a job.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, what was the training itself like? Did they prepare you? Was it, do you think, very different than the way they do the teaching now?

speaker: Marie Leitch Fisher
words: I don't know how they teach now. From the papers I pick up that the kids drop on the way home, they don't teach like they used to. From these papers I pick up that the kids go by and they've got an A on them, and I look through them, and there's a whole lot of mistakes on them. They can't spell, and they can't write, they've got big printing. And when I taught school, the kids went to the board and learned to write. They never did print, but of course, before I quit teaching, they had started printing. But I never bothered with that, because I couldn't see the value of printing first, then writing. And we had to teach Palmer Method of writing those days.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: When you were trained at Lewiston for teaching at the Normal, was the training very specific? Do they teach you just how to teach in a classroom, or what?

speaker: Marie Leitch Fisher
words: Yes, but they didn't. They taught the way it should be in a classroom, but after you got in a classroom, you had to remember what they told you, and then twist it to fit the, because these people that were training us were dedicated. I don't think that many of them had ever done very much rural school teaching, where you had eight grades in one room. And we had special courses in teaching English, and special courses in arithmetic, and special teachers to teach us how to teach spelling and everything else. But after you get out and start doing it while you just forget all that and do it your own way, that is, if you've got anything up here. What you're saying is it was more, it was theory and not practice. That's right. But I wasn't a bad primary teacher. By the time Christmas came, the kids could pick out different words. The smart ones, of course, the idiots, the morons, and the little people on the curve, you know, they couldn't. But the average kid knew a few words that they could pick out of the paper, and I'd never let them learn by the picture on the paper. They had to know the words because I taught phonics, and they could read pretty good. If you don't believe it, I asked Joe Holland. I had his kids in first grade. And Junior, his oldest boy, the one that got killed in the Army, he could almost read by Christmas. And by the time school was out, he was a pretty good reader. But he was a smart kid. But there were a lot of them because if a kid has phonics, he can set his own pace. He'd have to go around and wait for this sight reading. I don't know how I ever got kids to learn to read when I didn't teach phonics, but I must have. But now they're going back to phonics, somebody told me.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I've heard that too. I'm just wondering, did you have any special methods that you found that worked to get kids interested in reading? Or was it strict drills and that sort of thing?

speaker: Marie Leitch Fisher
words: No… i don't know.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you get, are there any games in that type of story?

speaker: Marie Leitch Fisher
words: Oh, sure. You know, that story of the three Billy Goats, the kids would read the story and then they'd act out. They'd be the three Billy Goats trying to get across the bridge that the troll was on. And then when you were teaching him how to, manners, why you'd have a kid knock at the door and the other kid would open the door and he'd come in blah blah blah. And I didn't do that very often, but months and a while we'd have things like that. And of course on Friday, afternoons, why they got a lot of artwork and spelling matches. Send them up the board and see what kid, give them a bunch of figures and see who could get through it quick. But those days we used to have contests between our school and dairy. Not only in athletics, but in spelling and arithmetic and stuff. Spelling and arithmetic and context were the only two contests we had. And they were fun because they just were.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Were these frequent get togethers for contests with theory? I mean, it was a common thing?

speaker: Marie Leitch Fisher
words: Well, it was for a year or two. It all depended greatly on who the teachers were. We found a got the point where we didn't go down, except they would have their track needs. But we had a superintendent that believed in developing their mental ability as well as their muscles. So we had them then. Of course, the dairy superintendent, I don't even remember who he was, cooperated. Of course, it only happened probably once a year, but then the kids got a lot of fun preparing for it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was it the same kind of thing in those days that nowadays you really do get the feeling that athletics is more important than schooling a lot of the time? Was it that way then too? Was athletics stressed so much?

speaker: Marie Leitch Fisher
words: Not in our schools. The idea was to get through all those books and pass into the next grade, and you didn't do that out playing basketball. Of course, I don't know about high school, but they were very basketball minded. And of course, everybody liked athletics. They never had enough kids to have a football team, but they always had good basketball teams, girl teams, some boy teams. And Bovill had the prettiest girls in the whole Latah County. I've heard that before.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: That's really true, huh?

speaker: Marie Leitch Fisher
words: Yes, it really is. They were just awfully...well, they were above average for good looks. We only had one or two fat ones, and even the fat ones were nice looking in the face. But the Lancaster, the Phillips, I don't have any pictures around with those girls, but they...oh, I've got them somewhere. They'd take a month to dig them out of this trash. But they were good looking, yeah. Beautiful girls. And the boys were nice looking, but the girls were better looking.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, that's good. That's the way it should be. When you first came to Bovill, were all the primary grades together as one, or were there different classes?

speaker: Marie Leitch Fisher
words: Oh, they had the first and second grade together, in third and fourth grade, fifth and sixth, seventh and eighth. There were four grade teachers, and there were, I guess, three or four high school teachers.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was this an improvement for you as a teacher to be able to just teach two grades instead of teaching a whole eight in one grade?

speaker: Marie Leitch Fisher
words: Well, it was a lot easier. I'll tell you that. You didn't have half the work to do, and it was more fun in that you could... You didn't have to have one kid teaching another. You could do it all yourself. I don't know. I enjoyed some of those one-room schools a lot, too, though. Especially one out here out in Lewiston somewhere. Someday I'm going to take the car and go out and see if I can find that school. You went out to Web Bridge, or you went out to that web post office, and you went up in those hills somewhere, and there's two roads after you leave Web Store, and I don't know which one I went on.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I'm surprised that you enjoyed the one-room school. I would think that for a teacher to deal with eight grades at once must just about be the limit.

speaker: Marie Leitch Fisher
words: But listen, I didn't find it in Bovill the first eight years I taught there. But if you're the teacher in a one-room school, boy, you are somebody the kids respect you. They never tried the smart-alecky things these kids in town tried. Why, if I'd been teaching anywhere and the kids had talked back to me like they do to these people now, I'd have broken their necks. Because those days you could spank kids. Of course, sometimes some of the people didn't like it very well because their little darlings got spanked, but they couldn't do anything about it. I wouldn't teach school now for all the tea in China.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did each teacher have to develop her own way of dealing with the problems of kids rebelling or not paying attention to you?

speaker: Marie Leitch Fisher
words: Yes… there was never any rebellion in those one-room schools because school was fun for most of those country kids. They got away from home and they got in with other kids, and they enjoyed school.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you feel that you had to be very strict with them?

speaker: Marie Leitch Fisher
words: No. Not the way you do in a town school. I know when I'd had seven or eight years experience before I went to Bovill, so I said, I usually tell them the first morning how this was school, and that I knew all their tricks. If they had been good, I'd be good. If they were going to be mean, I knew lots more mean ways than they did. I got it across that what I said was going to be, that was it. So I had very little trouble with the primary grades or the other ones either. I know I got awful mad at the superintendent one time because he spanked one of my kids. I felt if the kid needed spanking, I was the one to spank him, but the superintendent did it. He didn't make any friends influence any people either. He only stated that in all that year he left because the kid didn't need a spanking in the first place. And if he needed one, I was the one to give it to him, but I didn't get the chance prof did it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I imagine that he must have, that being a teacher in a school, well you will first, you were saying before that the first seven or eight years in Bovill, you say there was no discipline problem?

speaker: Marie Leitch Fisher
words: No, the first seven or eight years when I was teaching in the country schools, there was never any discipline problem.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did it take you a matter of time to establish yourself in Bovill as a... No, as a person that was going to be there, someone that was, you say the teacher didn't have the same kind of status in a town as she did in the country.
